description: Trepanation is the deliberate removal of a piece of the skull vault by scraping, grooving or drilling, first with stone tools. Healed bone edges show that many patients survived. description: Antiseptic surgery applied germ theory to wounds. uncertainty: Ignaz Semmelweis had cut childbed-fever deaths in Vienna by handwashing in 1847, before germ theory, but his explanation was not accepted. The shift from antiseptic to aseptic technique took place gradually in the 1880s-1890s.

description: Oral rehydration therapy treats the dehydration of diarrhoeal diseases such as cholera with a drink of clean water, salts and glucose. Glucose helps the gut absorb sodium, and water follows, even during infection. Trials in Dhaka and Calcutta in the late 1960s showed that it worked, and during the 1971 Bangladesh refugee crisis it sharply reduced cholera deaths.
uncertainty: The physiological basis (sodium-glucose co-transport) was established in the early 1960s by several groups; global uptake depended on health-worker programmes from the late 1970s.

description: Biomedical research is the continuing, organised effort to understand disease at the level of genes, cells and populations and to turn that understanding into treatment. Since the late twentieth century it has drawn on genome sequencing, large clinical trials and computing. Its results arrive unevenly: some conditions became treatable or preventable, while others, including many dementias, still resist.
uncertainty: As a repeatable node it stands for open-ended research rather than a dated discovery.

description: Endocrinology studies hormones, chemical messengers that glands release into the blood. In London in 1902, William Bayliss and Ernest Starling identified secretin, often called the first hormone; Starling introduced the word hormone in 1905. In 1922 a diabetic patient, Leonard Thompson, received insulin purified by James Collip, after work by Frederick Banting and Charles Best in John Macleod's laboratory.

claims: 1922 first insulin patient Leonard Thompson; Collip purification
Banting and Best in Macleod's laboratory

uncertainty: Gland extracts were used earlier (thyroid extract for myxoedema, 1891). Credit for insulin was disputed within the team; sources differ on who did what.

description: Immunology studies the body's defences against infection. In Berlin in 1890, Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburō showed that immunised animals produced blood antitoxins against diphtheria or tetanus toxins, and that such serum could protect others, founding serum therapy. In 1901 Karl Landsteiner used the clumping of red cells by serum to define blood groups, later central to transfusion.

claims: Behring and Kitasato 1890 antitoxins, Berlin Hygiene Institute
Behring and Kitasato 1890 antitoxins, Berlin Hygiene Institute

uncertainty: Immunology has several roots (Metchnikoff's cellular theory, Ehrlich's antibody theory). A contemporary critique held that Behring was anticipated by Japanese workers, and Ehrlich's methods were needed for an effective serum.

description: Sulfonamides were among the first synthetic drugs to treat bacterial infections inside the body. At Bayer in Germany, Gerhard Domagk found in 1932 that the dye Prontosil was far more effective than earlier dyes; results appeared in 1935. Researchers in Paris then showed that the active part was sulfanilamide. In 1936 Leonard Colebrook sharply reduced childbed-fever deaths with sulfonamides.

claims: Paris researchers identified sulfanilamide as the active part (late 1935)

uncertainty: Bayer was then part of IG Farben, and the chemists Klarer and Mietzsch synthesised the dye; sources differ on how credit is shared. Ehrlich's arsenical Salvarsan (1910) was an earlier synthetic antimicrobial, against syphilis.
